name: Erythromycin (acne)

lead: Topical erythromycin 2% is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. It is used for fewer red pimples in mild-to-moderate acne and is a long-established option, introduced in 1952.

It binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis, reducing acne-associated bacteria and the inflammation they drive. Reference sources describe it as typically combined with benzoyl peroxide.

paras: It is applied to the skin as a solution, usually alongside benzoyl peroxide, which limits the development of antibiotic resistance. It is used as a prescribed course rather than indefinitely.
Local dryness, peeling, itching and redness occur, and hives are rare. Labels warn of antibiotic-associated colitis. Reference sources note the pairing with benzoyl peroxide is to limit resistance.

angle.text: Topical erythromycin reduces acne bacteria, which lowers inflammation and leaves fewer red pimples. It is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne, and people typically pair it with benzoyl peroxide to limit bacterial resistance.

lead: Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic applied to the skin to calm inflamed acne, the red papules and pustules that dominate the look of breakouts. By reducing acne-associated bacteria, it helps lessen active spots and the redness around them, so skin looks clearer and evener over time. It is a macrolide antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis, and a 2% topical solution is labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. [1][2]

Dermatology guidance describes topical antibiotics, erythromycin among them, as most often paired with benzoyl peroxide, which limits the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. [1][3][4] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline as part of acne care. [3] Wikipedia notes that resistance to topical macrolides such as erythromycin has risen worldwide with broad antibiotic use. [4]

Preventing breakouts matters for appearance beyond the spots themselves: Wikipedia reports that acne scarring is estimated to affect most people with acne, and that post-inflammatory darkening can persist for months or years in people with darker skin. [4] Erythromycin has been on the market since 1952.
infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia

paras: The US label for erythromycin topical solution 2% lists acne vulgaris as its indication. [2] Grokipedia describes it as used for mild to moderate inflammatory acne, usually combined with benzoyl peroxide. [1] Wikipedia lists erythromycin alongside clindamycin, metronidazole and sulfacetamide as topical antibiotics for mild to moderately severe acne, and says dermatologists prefer to use antibiotics in combination rather than alone. [4]

On T Nation, users discussing hormone-related breakouts have mentioned a prescription routine of benzoyl peroxide wash followed by an erythromycin pad, and another poster listed erythromycin among antibiotics that worked for friends but not for them. [5][6]

sections.h: Combination with benzoyl peroxide and resistance
paras: Wikipedia states that benzoyl peroxide does not appear to cause bacterial resistance, unlike antibiotics, and that pairing the two is common in dermatology. [4] The same article says topical and oral antibiotics should not be used together, and that long oral courses are paired with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid. [4] The 2024 AAD guideline provides the evidence-based framework for these recommendations. [3]

The label lists occasional local reactions: peeling, dryness, itching, erythema and oiliness, with eye irritation and skin tenderness also reported. [2] Urticarial reactions requiring steroid treatment have been reported. [2] The label carries a warning about pseudomembranous colitis, which has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents. [2] It lists pregnancy category B, noting no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women. [2]
Erythromycin binds the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit and halts protein synthesis; its effect is mainly bacteriostatic. [1]
Erythromycin was launched as Ilosone by Eli Lilly in 1952 and patented the following year.

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline, a systematic review with graded recommendations, strongly recommends topical antibiotics for acne, alongside benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and oral doxycycline. [3] Other trials of erythromycin in the literature concern non-acne conditions such as gastrointestinal and obstetric uses.

lore.intro: Erythromycin for acne appears only in passing in forum discussions of acne treatments on T Nation. [5][6]
